title: perceived vulnerability (prototype pollution)
description:
Triggered by: learnr/inst/lib/i18n/i18next.min.js

> The i18next package is vulnerable to Prototype Pollution. The deepExtend() function in utils.js allows any object property to be overwritten. A remote attacker with control over any Javascript objects used in the i18next framework may pollute all object prototypes resulting in Remote Code Execution (RCE) or Denial-of-Service (DoS).

For more information refer to: https://github.com/i18next/i18next/pull/1482

title: plotting hangs in exercises for rocker/rstudio versions 4.4.2+
description:
When running learnr documents simple plots (e.g. `plot(1:10`)) time out in exercise chunks under the following conditions:

- rocker/rstudio versions >=4.4.2 (4.4.1 and below work fine)
- document contains a plot
- there is no .html file existing from a previous render (if the html file exists, there's no problem)
- attempt to plot something in the exercise chunk (other code works fine, just plotting gets stuck)

We have seen this on multiple platforms using different docker images based on rocker/rstudio

### Reprex
````
---
title: "test-plots"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
```

## Plot Data

### Plot run by document

```{r, echo=TRUE}
plot(1:10)
```


### Plot exercise

```{r freeplay-exercise, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE}

```
````

### Steps to reproduce
1. Run container based on rocker/rstudio (and install learnr + dependencies as needed)
2. Open tutorial .Rmd and click "Run Document"
3. Try to create a plot using the exercise chunk.

### Docker Details
rocker/rstudio needs a few dependencies to get learnr running, and I had to add zlib1g-dev to get them to compile, so in order to test things out locally I did the following: 

1. Built new docker image, that only adds zlib1g-dev:

**Dockerfile:**
```
FROM rocker/rstudio:4.4.2

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y zlib1g-dev
```

2. Started up the container and ran install.packages(“learnr”)
3. Clicked "Run Document", and said yes when prompted to install stringi, stringr
4. Clicked "Run Document", and it hangs on plotting the first time it runs, succeeds the second (and hangs again if I delete the .html file)

If I do exactly the same setup but use rocker/rstudio:4.4.1 instead of 4.4.2, then plotting works fine.


Got any ideas what might be going on? I realize rocker/rstudio is fairly complex and is not directly related to learnr, but it's a pretty popular image and is useful for getting student set up to work in cloud environments.

I'm also not sure where/how I could see more informative error messages; learnr doesn't print anything to the RStudio console, so I'm feeling a bit stuck as to how I could try to track this down.

title: Running Python chunks in learnr on shinyapps.io
description:
I’m trying to use the learnr package to publish multilingual tutorials on shinyapps.io.

I’ve run into an issue specifically with using Python in these tutorials:
1. The Python path is correctly recognized on shinyapps.io.
2. I can run Python code from R using the reticulate package.
3. However, when using the Python engine in R Markdown chunks, it fails to run.

All chunks (including the Python ones) work perfectly when run locally using rmarkdown::run().

Here is a simplified version of the code I’m using:

~~~
---
title: "Python on learnr"
date: "`r format(Sys.time(),'%Y-%m-%d')`"
author: "tetlabo"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
options(dplyr.width = Inf, scipen = 1, digits = 4)
library(reticulate)
# use_python(python = "/usr/bin/python3", required = TRUE) # Python path on shinyapps.io
```

## Introduction

This file tests running Python in a learnr tutorial on shinyapps.io.

```{bash code01, exercise=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
which python3
```

The system recognizes Python.

```{r code02, exercise=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sys <- import("sys")
sys$version
```

Using reticulate works fine.

```{python code03, exercise=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
import sys
print(sys.version)
```

However, using the Python engine in R Markdown results in an error.
~~~

Here is the actual deployed tutorial:
https://9z2nv0-0-0.shinyapps.io/00_tutorial/

The error message I get in the chunk is:

> "An internal error occurred while setting up the exercise. Please try again or contact the tutorial author."

Unfortunately, this message is not informative enough to help me debug the problem.

Do you have any insight or suggestions on how to get Python chunks working in learnr tutorials deployed on shinyapps.io?

title: YAML options to customize included directories
description:
I 100% understand why you wouldn't want to expose the entire working directory to the shiny app that learnr builds, but I wish it were possible to have a bit more flexibility in specifying which directories, precisely, should be included. It would be nice to be able to specify something like, say, `img/` as the images folder for consistency with the rest of the codebase I'm working on and the sake of not having to duplicate files & images.

To me, it seems like there could be an option in the YAML header to provide a list of folders that should be accessible to/included in the output, and this would also allow somebody to *stop* files from being exposed from any unfortunately-named existing directories if they needed to. Are the 4 specific directory names a learnr constraint or a shiny constraint?

(Sorry if you first saw this as a comment on a closed issue--I'm new to learnr but, poking around, it seems like there are several other people putting learnr tutorials inside of existing codebases that are asking questions like this, so I figured I should open an issue.)

title: Progressive Reveal for Topics at Level 2 Header ##
description:
I've been writing business tutorials lately that require that all sections of content are completed before receiving a certification and generating an output of documents on the last page. 

It would be great to be able to use progressive reveal at the topic level so that the Level 2 headers aren't revealed in the table of contents until the previous topic's subtopics have been completed so no one just skips to the end and generates the completion certificate without going through the previous tutorial steps!

Enabled for the whole document as:
```
---
title: "business tutorial"
output:
  learnr::tutorial:
    theme: "flatly"
    progressive-topic: true
    allow-topic-skip: true
runtime: shiny_prerendered
```
And enabled or disabled for specific topics: 
```
## Topic { data-progressive-topic: true }
```

title: Option to precompile/render html
description:
## Issue
I'm working to deploy learnr tutorials using docker on fly.io. One thing I've noticed is that time to first render is quite high/buggy because the server must render the learnr tutorial the first time it's accessed. This is further exacerbated by using ephemeral docker containers that are torn down when usage is low and are later spun back up, requiring re-rendering all over again. Ephemeral containers are very useful in this particular case because it allows me to spin up high resource machines without worrying/forgetting to tear them down later when demand dies down.

## Feature request
 It might be possible to store the compiled tutorial in a persistent volume, but I think a better solution would be to be able to compile the learnr tutorial when building the docker image. I don't see any current way to do that, as I believe it's largely been the case that pre-rendering is incompatible when sharing tutorials so it has never been developed. However, this seems like a perfectly fine use case, as we have full control over the environment.  

I would be happy to help implement something like this if someone could point me in the right direction.

title: Error if `-solution` chunk has an unneeded `exercise.setup` option
description:
Using an `exercise.setup` option in a `-solution` results in an error if the chunk is not referenced in the `exercise.setup` option of another chunk.

```` rmd
---
title: "Tutorial"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
```

## Exercise 1

```{r exercise-1, exercise = TRUE}
```

```{r exercise-1-solution}
x <- 1
```

## Exercise 2

```{r exercise-2, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "exercise-1-solution"}
```

```{r exercise-2-solution, exercise.setup = "exercise-1-solution"}
y <- x + 1
```

## Exercise 3

```{r exercise-3, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "exercise-2-solution"}
```

```{r exercise-3-solution, exercise.setup = "exercise-2-solution"}
z <- x + y
```

````

``` r
rmarkdown::run("setup-chaining.Rmd")
#> processing file: setup-chaining.Rmd
#> Quitting from lines 35-36 (setup-chaining.Rmd)
#> Error: Chunk 'exercise-3-solution' is not being used by any exercise or exercise setup chunk.
#> Please remove chunk 'exercise-3-solution' or reference 'exercise-3-solution' with `exercise.setup = 'exercise-3-solution'`
```

<sup>Created on 2023-04-14 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This can cause problems for authors who are testing an unfinished exercise that uses setup chaining. They will have to remember not to add an `exercise.setup` option to `exercise-3-solution` until after they've written `exercise-4`.

Would it cause any issues if this threw a warning instead of an error?

title: Change default error message for `question_checkbox()`
description:
Can we change the default error message for `question_checkbox()` from
- `incorrect = "Incorrect"`
to something like
- `incorrect = "Incorrect. Be sure to select every correct answer."`?

`question_checkbox()` differs from `question_radio()` in that it allows for more than one correct answer—_and students must select every correct answer to pass_.  I've noticed several students assume that a checkbox question is a radio question. They select one correct answer and receive `"Incorrect!"`. They then switch to a different correct answer and also receive `"Incorrect!"`. This creates frustration, which I think we could solve by automatically including a nudge to look for multiple correct answers.

**Caveat**: the proposed message may not play well with `allow_retry = FALSE`. I don't think that's fatal, but I'm happy to entertain better messages 😄 .

title: Using global environment to pass variables between code chunks
description:
As I understand the code chunks being independent is a policy decision, however, for our application (student use during live statistics lectures) it is very limiting as we want students to see the results of their own code between different exercises not what we have hard-coded (which is what the setup chunks / chaines setup chunks currently allow for) and the exercises are complex enough that  several different approaches with different output should be possible.

We did find a workaround to save variables in a global environment in local files using a checker function but this seems to not work once uploaded on shiny.io. In a previous thread about this it was mentioned that allowing passing variables between code chunks would not be technically difficult - would it then be possible to let me know how I can maybe modify / overwrite that bit of  the learnr package's code for our project if there is still no interest in making this a generally available option?

```{r cars2}
```

```{r}
knitr::knit_code$get("cars")
knitr::knit_code$get("cars2")
```
````

We should investigate why learnr includes this constraint and then remove it if possible. It becomes a bigger issue if we use yaml-style chunk option comments, since they gobble one empty line after the YAML comments, requiring two empty lines after the chunk options.

title: Ensure forced exercise chunk options are applied to both chunk and global options
description:
When evaluation submitted code, we intend to force `eval = TRUE`, but having an explicit `eval = FALSE` on the exercise chunk causes the submitted code to be evaluated with `eval = FALSE`.

```r
ex <- mock_exercise(
  label = "ex",
  chunks = list(
    mock_chunk("ex", "1 + 1", exercise = TRUE, eval = FALSE)
  ),
  check = I("last_value")
)

# Note the `eval=FALSE` chunk option...
ex
#> ```{r "ex", eval=FALSE, exercise=TRUE}
#> 1 + 1
#> ```
res <- evaluate_exercise(ex, new.env())
str(res$feedback$checker_result)
#> List of 3
#> $ echo   : logi FALSE
#> $ comment: logi NA
#> $ error  : logi FALSE
```

(Note the additional bug that in this case we returned a `last_value` that comes from a setup chunk rather than the users code.)

Expected output:

```r
ex$chunks[[1]]$opts$eval <- TRUE
ex
#> ```{r "ex", eval=TRUE, exercise=TRUE}
#> 1 + 1
#> ```
res <- evaluate_exercise(ex, new.env())
res$feedback$checker_result
#> [1] 2
```

title: paritally editable exercises
description:
I cannot find the game any more but there was/is a javascript game where you have to escape a dungeon by editing javascript. The dungeon and the player's and enemies' movements are all javascript that is readable and partially editable by the player, sometimes you have to edit the dungeon layout and sometimes the movement of the player to escape.

The cool part is that you can see the entire code that generates the dungeon and the movement but you can *only edit a few lines* the rest of the code is static.

This would allow to make a function and you could force the user to only fill a specific argument or to only edit a single variable in a script. Being able to constrain a script this way would allow for much more complex exercises where the student has to understand some given code.

title: Feature request: MCQs that do not tell the student their response is incorrect
description:
We need a variant of multiple choice question that does not grade a user's responses wrong.

## Use Case: Make a guess

I commonly ask students to pre-think before instruction. I do this with a multiple choice question like, "Make a guess. What would happen if you ran `1 + `?" I would like to provide the student feedback based on their answer, but I would not like to indicate that any answer is wrong. i.e. with a red message and the word Incorrect. I would prefer that:
1. The correct answer is handled as is with a green background and the word Correct
2. Other answers are handled in a more neutral way: a neutral colored background and no Incorrect at the top of the message.

I have no opinion on the best syntax for specifying this.

title: Improve youtube and vimeo link-identifying regexps
description:
The current regexps for identifying YouTube and Vimeo links are designed to find links that are known candidates. For example, the YT regexp is good for extracting the embed ID from a known probable YT link. They don't however, include some baseline checks such as checking that the link is an `https?` link. It would be unusual, but it's still possible that something not intended to be used as a YT link (a base64-encoded image, for example) could be picked out as a YT link.

https://github.com/rstudio/learnr/blob/1c01ac258230cbe217eee16c77cc71924faab1d3/learnr-js/tutorial/tutorial.js#L404-L405

[Our docs state](https://pkgs.rstudio.com/learnr/articles/learnr.html?q=youtube#videos) that the whole link should be used, so I think it'd be okay for us to add in `^http` to the regexp. Alternatively, we could find a more robust regular expression.

title: Create separate method for rendering exercise HTML
description:
I'm moving this to its own issue because it's a larger task than where I originally proposed it. In short, we could reduce complexity and improve extensibility and maintainability of the exercise components by

1. Using the knitr hooks to create the exercise object and set required knitr chunk options
2. Using a separate function to format the exercise component into its initial HTML format

_Originally posted by @gadenbuie in https://github.com/rstudio/learnr/issues/548#issuecomment-902186996_

> I think the solution here is to remove the complexity around the knitr hooks. Instead of individually writing the tutorial support chunks, we should have the `exercise` chunk write _all_ of the HTML for the exercise and then we'll disable any kind of output from the support chunks. In addition to simplifying the logic, this would let us re-use chunks between exercises.

> Alternatively, if we decouple hints and solutions and let the shiny app control whether the solution button is present (and what that solution is), then we wouldn't even need to write the solution chunk html into the document.

title: Document that setting tutorial ID is required on RStudio Cloud
description:
From [RStudio Community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/learnr-tutorials-not-saving-in-rstudio-cloud/128320):

> Some students are not able to install the tutorial package onto their computer, so I setup a Rstudio cloud project for them to use. However when they stop the session after they work on it for a little bit (to save computational time and stay under the free time limits), it does not save their work. 
> Is this a bug?

The tutorial progress storage is based on the tutorial's ID. If your [tutorial doesn't explicitly set the ID](https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/articles/publishing.html#tutorial-identifiers), then a default value is chosen based on a few things. On RStudio Cloud, the port of the application path encoded in the URL where the user accesses the running tutorial. learnr will encorporate that port in the default tutorial identifier, but unfortunately this port number changes with each run.

Adding the following to the YAML frontmatter of those tutorials this will clear up problems for your users, even on RStudio Cloud:

```yaml
tutorial:
  id: math350_lrt_1_introR
  version: 1 # change the version when you want to invalidate past progress
```

Note that if you release a totally different version of the tutorial and want any one with stored progress to reset, you can change the version value (which can be an arbitrary string).

title: Add special unparseable message for curly quotes (and other Unicode characters?)
description: Currently, all unparseable user input returns the following message: > It looks like this might not be valid R code. R cannot determine how to turn your text into a complete command. You may have forgotten to fill in a blank, to remove an underscore, to include a comma between arguments, or to close an opening ", ', ( or { with a matching ", ', ) or }. This works well for code the student has typed incorrectly, but doesn't help with another common problem: students copying and pasting code with automatic Unicode formatting. For example, if the code `str_detect("test", "t.+t")` is copied into Zoom chat, it will be reformatted with curly quotes as `str_detect(“test”, “t.+t”)`. The student may never notice the change, and be confused that their code is returning an error. I propose adding the following messages to be displayed when a student's code is unparseable and contains a non-ASCII character. #### Code with curly quotes > It looks like this might not be valid R code. Your code contains curly quotation marks (“”) when R expects straight quotation marks (""). This can happen when you copy and paste code from another source. Try deleting the quotation marks in your code and retyping them manually. #### Code with other non-ASCII characters In this case, a student has copied a Unicode minus sign instead of an ASCII [hyphen-minus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyphen-minus): > It looks like this might not be valid R code. Your code contains the following special character: −. Sometimes your code may contain a special character that looks like a regular character, especially if you copy and paste from another source. Try deleting the special character from your code and retyping it manually.

title: Write all hints in chunks
description:
Now that we have a data structure for describing the interactive exercises, we're still missing hints. The primary problem is that they can be added via supporting R chunks or by using a `<div>` with an id that ends in `-hint`.

I'd like to restructure the hints so that they are always written in chunks in a tutorial. I'd also like to build on this to have the pop-up display all hints, not just code hints. We'd support any other language via knitr chunk engine, or we could use a chunk option on `markdown`, `md`, or `html` chunks — `exercise.hint.render = TRUE` — that would render the markdown or display the literal HTML in the pop-up.

title: `allow_skip: false` allows next section on empty console
description:
### Issue 

Current behavior of learnr exercises with YAML `progressive: true` and `allow_skip: false` doesn't condition the access to a next section based on the code submitted.

When clicking Continue / Next topic before any interaction with the exercise, the following message appears:

> You must complete the exercise in this section before continuing.

This is a bit misleading as clicking on the **Run code**  button on any code or even on an empty console unlocks access to the next section. 

I understand conditioning button behavior on code run in exercises chunks might be tricky, but it should at least check that users didn't just click **Run code** on an empty console.

## Steps to reproduce

Initiate a basic learnr tutorial (with Rstudio: File > New file > R Markdown... > from Template > interactive tutorial).

Replace YAML:

```
---
output: learnr::tutorial
---
```

With

```
---
output: 
  learnr::tutorial:
    progressive: true
    allow_skip: false
---
```

Click **Run code** on the first exercise without typing any code in to mark the exercise as completed and unlock access to the next section.

## Session info
learnr 0.10.1.9017 on Win10 machine

title: Rerunning tutorial inside R package enables code evaluation for hints.
description:
# Problem
I created a package, which includes functions, datasets and tutorials. The latter works when starting a **new R session** and running a tutorial for the **first time**.
After closing the tutorial (clicking the `stop` button) and restarting it again, all code chunks which contain hints are now evaluated and throw errors, for example, the following code chunk:

> \```{r take-sqrt-hint-2}
> sqrt(...)
> \```

results in the following error message:

> **Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : '...' used in an incorrect context**

Restarting the R session and running the tutorial enables the tutorial. Stopping it and rerunning it seems to allow code chunk evaluation for hints again and breaks the tutorial.

This seems to be only a problem when tutorials are in packages and using the following to load them:

```r
learnr::run_tutorial("tutorial_name", package="pkg_name")
```

Once I close the browser, the console still shows that it is listening to the IP address where the tutorial ran. Not sure why it keeps on running, but I assume it does not detect that I closed the tutorial? This likely explains this odd behaviour.

# Current Fix
I added `eval=FALSE` to all code chunks, which are hints. This solves the problem.

Thanks in advance for any help with this. I assume there must be a more straightforward fix to this than what I currently do. In my case, hints are hardly ever 'full' code that can be run but progressively builds up to the final solution.

title: Disable code completion on lines that start with # (e.g. comment lines)
description:
I've been watching a bunch of screen recordings of my research participants interacting with learnr, and something I've noticed is how distracting/frustrating it is for the otherwise helpful code completion to pop up when users are writing comments. 

Perhaps there could be an option to disable code completion for lines that start with #?

I totally understand that getting users to write their own comments within a learnr exercise chunk is not a common activity for other users of learnr so this is probably not a feature worth investing in 😄

title: Intermitent parse error trailing garbage error
description:
I'm using a package of learnr tutorials for teaching that I wrote (https://github.com/profandyfield/discovr ).

Some students intermitently get the following error when the click 'start tutorial'.

```
Error: parse error: trailing garbage

          ":{},"value":["0.10.1"]}]}]} {"type":"list","attributes":{},

                     (right here) ------^

Execution halted
```

I had similar issues last year as well which remained unresolved. I can't post a reporducible example because we can't reporduce it: We can't see any consistent predictors of when it happens or for whom. It feels impossible to debug but I also don't really understand the process of what happens when someone clicks the 'start tutorial' button (other than it reneders my RMD into a tutortial ... or how it uses a stored html file when a tutorial starts or how a stored html might become corrupt.

We have students who, for example, load a tutorial successfully using the RStudio tutorials pane, but then next time they load it they get this error. Based on my explorations last year I assume it's an error with the html renedering. Consistent with this assumption if we (a) manually delete the html of the problematic tutorial from the package library on their system, or (b) force a reinstall (which would also clear the html files) the problem goes away. However, it can return (for the same student).

I don't know if this is a bug, and I appreciate (really I do having tried to workiit out for over a year) how impossible it is to have a solution when we can't reliably reproduce the issue, but I would really appreciate some pointers about why this might be happening - like, some options to explore or some better understanding of the rendering process and why it might fail when it has succeeded before. Could this be down to user input in a previous session using the tutorial? Could it be to do with strange text in my hints? Is there something I can do within the tutorial to prevent it (I currently don't error catch any code that students type into exercises). Any useful pointers?

title: Setup chunks for pre-evaluated exercises: source hidden but output is shown
description:
When an exercise is pre-evaluated with `exercise.eval = TRUE`, the setup chunks are all evaluated as well and the output is shown. But `echo=FALSE` is enforced on the setup chunk, so it's not possible to override this behavior.

<details><summary>Reprex</summary>

````
---
title: "Tutorial"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
```

## Topic 1

```{r two-plus-two-setup, echo=TRUE}
x <- 2
x
```

```{r two-plus-two, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval = TRUE}
x + 2
```
````

</details>

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5420529/131524138-2e932f5c-2d19-479a-8d06-27cf1a918b54.png)


I see two options for when `exercise.eval=TRUE`:

- Respect the actual chunk options, e.g. let `echo=TRUE` or `include=FALSE` on the setup chunk be used.
- _Always_ hide output from exercise support chunks, and only show the pre-rendered of the exercise chunk specifically.

I like the second option best as it's most consistent with our other modes. 

OTOH, the first option can be used as a way to have setup chunks appear in both the exercise and the pre-rendered tutorial, rather than using `ref.label` or other chunk-repeating techniques. I'm less excited about this option since it requires pre-evaluating the exercise code, which may contain errors or be incomplete, and it's a rather large side-effect to result from setting the `exercise.eval` chunk option.

title: Exercise checking should include an argument indicating which type of check is being perfomed
description:
If we add a ~`type`~ `stage` argument to the function signature of the exercise checker, `learnr` can communicate which checking step is being performed.

Practically speaking this would allow `gradethis` to relax the "always return a grade" constraint for code checking, which would allow grading to do a first-pass code check before full evaluation.

The impact would be small for exercise checking functions that include `...`. Alternatively, the checking step can be inferred from the values of particular arguments as described in [Exercises - Custom Checking](https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/exercises.html#Custom_Checking), but it'd be cleaner to simply tell the checker what step is being performed.

cc @schloerke

title: Multiple Choice: Individual feedback for all answer options
description:
It is essential to give individual feedback for all answer options, either correct or incorrect. Rich feedback is an important feature of Multiple-Choice Questions (MCs) because teachers do not want only to give individual feedback for wrong answers ("distractors") but also often want to explain why correct options are correct.

As far as I can see, individual feedback for all answer options is not possible for MCs in the `learnr` package. Only for wrong answers, a message can be displayed if students choose this wrong option. Therefore, the overall false feedback wording in `try_again` or `incorrect` must cover all possible combinations,  including partly correct answers. The result is awkward wording that can never cover all combinations.

Look for instance of the pizza topping example. 

```{r checkbox-example}
question(
  "Select all the toppings that belong on a Margherita Pizza:",
  answer("tomato", correct = TRUE),
  answer("mozzarella", correct = TRUE),
  answer("basil", correct = TRUE),
  answer("extra virgin olive oil", correct = TRUE),
  answer("pepperoni", message = "Great topping! ... just not on a Margherita Pizza"),
  answer("onions"),
  answer("bacon"),
  answer("spinach"),
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  try_again = "Be sure to select all toppings!"
)
```

The general wrong feedback "try_again = 'Be sure to select all toppings!'" does not make sense if students choose all correct options with one or more wrong options. General wrong feedback like "Incorrect" is not a solution as choosing several correct options (but not all) is better characterized as "Only partly correct" than incorrect. I could not think of wording for a general wrong answer which covers all possible outcomes.

Another side effect of the MC design in `learnr` is that you cannot grade the answer partially correct. Neither fine grading with points is possible by (for instance) calculating the chosen correct options minus the chosen the wrong options.

I believe that MCs need individual feedback for all chosen options and fine grading. To demonstrate the difference and how it could be implemented, I have [prepared an example of the pizza toppings MC](https://peter.baumgartner.name/testseiten/h5p-multiple-choice-learnr/#h5p-pizza) with precisely the same `learnr` choices but designed with [H5P](https://h5p.org/). 
 
 > H5P is a free and open-source content collaboration framework based on JavaScript. H5P is an abbreviation for HTML5 Package and aims to make it easy for everyone to create, share and reuse interactive HTML5 content.
 
If you scroll the MC exercise down, then you see a screenshot that demonstrates that teachers can set in H5P different options and messages for **every** choice:
 
- correct or incorrect
- feedback if the answer was chosen
- feedback if the answer was not chosen
- help text for the option

But for my example, more important: After answering, students get feedback in three different ways:
- which options were chosen correctly
- which options were chosen incorrectly 
- how many choices would be correct

Teachers can optionally calculate points via correct/incorrect options or give maximal just one point by requiring that all possibilities be chosen correctly.

So my questions are: 
- Did I overlook something, and my perception of the feedback problem in `learnr` is wrong, or could it be solved with the actual design?
- If not: Wouldn't it be nice to change the somewhat restricted design of `learnr` MCs?

PS.: I'm using the GitHub version of `learnr`: 0.10.1.9009.

title: Using a solution chunk as a chained setup chunk hides the solution in the UI
description:
In the example below, the second exercise uses the solution to the first exercise as its setup chunk, via the chunk option `exercise.setup = "first-solution"`. As a result, the Solution button is not included in the UI since the solution code isn't added to the HTML. ````markdown --- title: "Tutorial" output: learnr::tutorial runtime: shiny_prerendered --- ```{r setup, include=FALSE} library(learnr) knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE) ``` ## Topic 1 ```{r first, exercise = TRUE} x <- 1 x + 1 ``` ```{r first-solution} x <- 2 x + 1 ``` ```{r second, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup="first-solution"} x + 2 ``` ```{r second-solution} x + 2 ``` ```` The HTML output for the first exercise in the above is missing the code for the solution. ```html 
x <- 1
x + 1
``` The problem doesn't occur if a new chunk is created duplicating the solution chunk: ```` ```{r first-solution2, ref.label="first-solution"} ``` ```{r second, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup="first-solution2"} x + 2 ``` ````

title: Fix usage of bootstrap panels for quizes and questions
description:
Currently, quizzes with multiple questions created via this markdown ````markdown ```{r quiz} quiz( question("Which package contains functions for installing other R packages?", answer("base"), answer("tools"), answer("utils", correct = TRUE), answer("codetools") ), question("Which of the R packages listed below are used to create plots?", answer("lattice", correct = TRUE), answer("tools"), answer("stats"), answer("grid", correct = TRUE) ) ) ``` ```` result in this HTML markup ```html

Quiz

``` The "broken" part is the usage of `.panel-heading` outside `.panel`. In the browser, the `.panel-heading` is pulled out of the `

` tag, but it still remains outside a `.panel`. One approach would be to create nested panels with the quiz title in the `.panel-heading` of the parent `.panel`. On the other hand, I personally don't mind that the quiz questions aren't inside a parent container, although there's a strong argument that semantically they should be. We might also want to rewrite the usage of `.panel` in questions to place the question prompt inside a `.panel-heading` div. But that may end up restricting usage of HTML in question prompts, which would be less preferable.

title: question_numeric with tolerance
description:
The `question_numeric` does not take a tolerance argument, but the comparision of the answer and user input is evaluated using a tolerance of `1e-10`: https://github.com/rstudio/learnr/blob/master/R/question_numeric.R#L99
It would be nice if this tolerance could be specified, e.g. `tol = 1e-10`.
This could be achived by replacing L99 by: `if (isTRUE(all.equal(ans_val, value, tolerance = question$options$tol)))`, adding `tol = tol` after L59 and adding `tol = 1e-10` as the default argument to `question_numeric`

title: Feature request: "Start Over" Button for all header level 3 of a section
description:
The [OpenIntro ims-tutorial](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims-tutorials/) provides a huge and comprehensive interactive course with the `learnr` package. Each book chapter is a tutorial on its own. Each chapter has several voluminous Rmd files, and each header in the table of contents region of the file often consists of many sections themselves (header level 3). 

Until now, it is only possible to start over an exercise chunk or the whole tutorial file. I think in those comprehensive cases, a "Start Over" button for all the progressively revealed sections would be of educational advantage. Students would not need to start the complete chapter from scratch but could repeat just one part.

title: Feature request: Run only selected lines of an exercise chunk
description:
Many times I have seen exercise chunks where a complex task is broken down into several steps. The code snippets consist of some prefilled parts and some parts with underscores to be substituted by the student's code. The following illustrating screenshot is taken from a [lesson of the OpenIntro project](https://openintro.shinyapps.io/ims-02-summarizing-and-visualizing-data-02/#section-density-plots-vs.-boxplots).

![task-with-several-steps](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/24394304/114741748-6060d980-9d4b-11eb-9057-9043e4aedcca.png)


In those cases, where a task is broken down into several steps, it would be beneficial from an educational perspective when students could experiment and see if a part of their solution already works. At the moment, students have to cut those parts not ready for evaluation, try their solution, and then continue their work with pasting the code snippet from the clipboard to the exercise environment.  

An alternative could be to provide students with an extra empty exercise chunk as a sandbox to try their experiments.

But the easiest solution would be to run just a part of the exercise chunk as possible in RStudio by selecting code lines.

I do not know if this feature request could be implemented (easily), but it would provide a great enhancement.

title: Disable rerun of code execution at application start-up
description:
My team has searched around to see if this is possible, but we don't think it is.

Currently, when you open a learnr application, each of the exercise blocks executes to restore the results from the last session. When a learnr application gets larger, this can become quite intensive - particularly if the application will be used in a larger environment with a shared external evaluator, and in turn cause exercise chunks to hang while waiting for others' code to finish.

An ideal scenario would be to restore the code executed to the exercise chunk, but not rerun the exercise itself.

title: Require users to answer questions when allow_skip = FALSE
description:
As pointed out on [RStudio Community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/can-you-prevent-skipping-questions-in-learnr/97960), the `allow_skip = FALSE` option only applies to _exercises_ and does not include questions.

> In the learnr documentation, it is clear that by default learners must complete *exercises* before continuing, and there is the option to disable this globally or by chunk with `allow_skip` .
> 
> By default, it seems as though *questions* can be skipped. Is there any way to require completing questions before continuing?


https://github.com/rstudio/learnr/blob/6694842d8b9a74fbff92ef8a64a49adcc5a30199/inst/rmarkdown/templates/tutorial/resources/tutorial-format.js#L181-L182

title: Helpers to handle local data files and file setup
description:
A few options to handle common usage of data files in learnr exercises, such as those described in #99

1. Make the `data/` directory special and copy it into the exercise temp dir
2. Provide a helper function that knows the absolute path of the `data/` dir that can be used in the setup chunk
3. Provide a chunk option, e.g. `exercise.files`, that will copy a vector of relative (to `tutorial.Rmd`) file paths into the exercise temp dir

The problem with all of the above is that it would be very hard to ensure that external evaluation will work correctly without serializing and sending the files with each submission.

```{r setup}
library(learnr)
```

```{sql sql-ex, connection = starwarsdb::starwars_connect(), exercise = TRUE}
select * from people;
```
````

because the `connection` chunk option is evaluated and serialized into

```
connection = new("duckdb_connection", dbdir = character(0), 
  conn_ref = <pointer: 0x7fe936fc8080>, driver = new("duckdb_driver", 
    database_ref = <pointer: 0x7fe936f7a9f0>, dbdir = ":memory:", 
    read_only = FALSE), debug = FALSE)
```

which is broken by the `<pointer: 0x7fe936fc8080>`.

When this happens, the only way is to create the connection in the global setup chunk and reference its object name as a character string. Even using the connection object name unquoted will cause it to be serialized.

````
---
title: "SQL"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

## Using SQL

```{r setup}
library(learnr)
con <- starwarsdb::starwars_connect()
```

```{sql sql-ex, connection = "con", exercise = TRUE}
select * from people;
```
````

We might want to protect this option from serialization. I also wonder what would be the best approach for handling connection pooling or serving tutorials for many users at once from the same host.

title: Make tutorials printable

description:
In the tutorials I write I often have essay questions. I have a custom question type for this purpose. But I realize that the current `question_text()` will support essays: it's just a matter of calling it with the right arguments, e.g.

````
```{r essay-14}
question_text("What do you think about this?", 
   answer("nice", correct=TRUE), allow_retry=TRUE, incorrect=NULL, 
   try_again_button = "Edit answer.", options=list(nrows=6))
```
````

I realize that this is not what `question_text()` was originally intended for, but it works fine and the change is very simple: change `textInput` to `textAreaInput` and perhaps allow the number of rows to be set via the question options.

```
question_ui_initialize.learnr_text <- function(question, value, ...) {
  textAreaInput( 
    question$ids$answer,
    label = question$question,
    placeholder = question$options$placeholder,
    value = value,
    rows = question$options$nrows %||% 1  # Keep it small for backward compatibility
  )
}
```

title: Anchor sections in rmarkdown 2.5 with learnr
description:
rmarkdown 2.5 introduced a new anchor sections feature that adds `#` characters when hovering over heading text. Unfortunately, there are a few places where this feature impacts learnr tutorials.

1. **Tabsets**. Because tabsets are initialized _after_ the anchor sections JS is run, anchors are added to the tab headings. They overflow the tab container and add vertical space between the tabs and the content.

   The easy fix would be to hide the anchors in the tabset styles in the tutorial template.

   ```css
   .tabset > ul.nav-tabs > li > .anchor-section {
     display: none;
   }
   ```

   I can PR this if this works. Otherwise, the alternative would be to ensure that tabs are initialized before anchors are added.

1. Empty headings used to add pauses, like the empty level-3 headings often used in tutorials, end up with an anchor even though there's no text. This may be fixed upstream https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/issues/1937

1. As far as I can tell, it's not possible to link into a level-3 heading or below using URL hashes. This makes sense, since those sections may not be revealed until a user has worked through some exercises first. For this reason, in addition to the above, it may make sense to disable `anchor_sections` by default for learnr tutorials. I can also PR this change if desired.

title: `tutorial_options()` doesn't set the default options
description:
When calling `tutorial_options()`, the default values of the options are not set. 

For example, `exercise.diagnostics = TRUE` is a default value, but when calling `tutorial_options()`, this value isn't set. 

It happens because the options are set using `if (!missing())`, but even with a default value for the parameter, the argument will still be missing when `tutorial_options()` alone is called. 

How to fix: use `if (!is.null())` instead of `missing()`.

(will PR this change soon)

title: Allow students to annotate text
description:
When we seek advice from online education content designers, they emphasize that students pay more attention to text when they have the ability to interact with it, for example by highlighting, underlining, or inserting notes/comments.

Students currently cannot interact with the text in learnr documents, but we keenly want them to pay attention to the text. 

To act on this advice, we should
1. Make it possible for readers to
    + Highlight portions of text in a learnr document 
    + Insert comments into a learnr document
2. Save and replay highlights and comments for the students in the same way that we save and replay their progress
3. Warn students when they click Start Over that they will lose their highlights/comments (or better yet retain their highlights/comments when they click start over)

title: 'Empty' exercise chunks aren't treated as exercises
description:
Running the tutorial below yields a misleading error of:

```r
Error in is_code_identical(user, solution) : 
  No solution is provided for this exercise.
```

This is because the `foo` chunk isn't being treated as an exercise, so the `foo-check` is being evaluated outside of a `grade_learnr()` context. Adding an empty line to the `foo` chunk fixes the problem, but either a more informative error should be thrown, or it should "just work"

````
---

output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

library(learnr)
library(gradethis)
tutorial_options(exercise.checker = grade_learnr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
```

sum(1)

```{r foo-check}
grade_code()

It would be nice to have an sound to alert users when they make an error in a Quiz Question. Similarly, a celebratory sound if they get it correct.

           answer("1",correct = F),

           answer("2", correct = T),
           answer("-1.9952",correct = F),
           allow_retry = T,
           incorrect = rep(beep(2),4)
  )
)
```

title: Question requiring at leat one correct (instead of all correct)
description:
I haven't seen this request, but maybe I didn't look carefully enough: I tried to make a `question` where several answers are considered correct, and the behaviour I obtained was that the only correct solution was to check all correct answers. My intention was that it would be considered correct if at least one of the correct answers was checked (and none of the wrong answers).

For instance:
```
question("Select at least one TRUE expression",
         answer("`2 < 4`", correct = TRUE, message = "`!FALSE` is also correct"),
         answer("`!FALSE`", correct = TRUE, message = "`2 < 4` is also correct"),
         answer("`TRUE & (2 < 1)`"),
         allow_retry = TRUE
         )
```

Selecting only one of the correct answers is considered wrong. What would be nice is an `any_correct` option that would result in the desired behaviour.

A related feature would be to allow multiple choice square check boxes even when only one answer is correct, in order to avoid giving the hint that only one answer is correct.

title: Horizontal layout option for `question_radio()`
description:
Motivation:

Pedagogically, it can sometimes be useful to provide a long list of distractors. It's also helpful to be able to ask many short questions. Regrettably, the question options in `{learnr}` lay things out in a vertical format. The result is visually confusing.

Proposal:

I propose a layout option like this:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/532653/82825048-1d1a2580-9e70-11ea-8277-7d3c59754098.png)

Actually, I'd prefer if the submit/try-again buttons were inline with the question prompt, to save further vertical space. 

I'm implemented the above via an `inline` field passed via the general-purpose `options=` argument. Then a very small change in `radio_question.R` will provide the option while preserving the default behavior ...

```r
question_ui_initialize.learnr_radio <- function(question, value, ...) {
  choice_names <- answer_labels(question)
  choice_values <- answer_values(question)

  radioButtons(
    question$ids$answer,
    label = question$question,
    inline = ifelse("inline" %in% names(question$options),
                 question$options$inline,
                 FALSE),
    choiceNames = choice_names,
    choiceValues = choice_values,
    selected = value %||% FALSE # setting to NULL, selects the first item
  )
}
```

title: rstudio.cloud and shared workspaces
description:
Hello,
Many thanks for your `learnr` package! It is really useful in teaching! I'm sorry that I deviate from your issue template, but I try to keep things as reproducible as possible.

In teaching R, we use rstudio.cloud and learnr. On rstudio.cloud we have a workspace for a group of students. Students are copying a project that contains a learnr tutorial. Every student has an own copy of this project and walks through the learnr tutorial by pressing `run document` in rstudio.

However, we got multiple issues with this set up. In a running learnr tutorial R sessions crashed or exercises could not be executed because R indicated that it is still running and cannot execute a new task.

I think I was able to trace the problem:

- learnr thinks it is running on a local computer (`Listening on http://127.0.0.1:3699`), thus uses a local storage.
- Local storage is stored in `file.path(rappdirs::user_data_dir(), "R", "learnr", "tutorial", "storage")` (storage.R, l. 277).
- `rappdirs::user_data_dir()` points in rstudio.cloud to `/home/rstudio-user/.local/share`.
- It appears to me that `/home/rstudio-user/.local/share` is shared between projects in the same workspace or projects that are derived from the same project that are running at the same time.
- `user_id` in rstudio.cloud is the same for every user.
- Thus, learnr objects are saved and loaded from the same place by different rstudio.cloud users.

I assume that other users of rstudio.cloud could run into the same problem. So maybe it is helpful for you to know about this issue?

We circumvented this behavior by using an own local storage provider. I'm not really sure whether this is an issue in learnr or in rstudio.cloud. So I can move this issue if this is not the correct place.

Best,
mutlusun

title: store/clear_exercise_setup_chunks only works once per process
description:
The first time you run rmarkdown::run on a doc, you get the correct ordering of `clear` followed by `store` later on.

```
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::clear_exercise_setup_chunks()
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
session$onSessionEnded(function() {
        learnr:::session_stop_event(session)
      })
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::store_exercise_setup_chunk("__setup__", c("library(learnr)", "knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)", "", "tutorial_event_recorder <- function(tutorial_id, tutorial_version, user_id, ", "                                    event, data) {", "  cat(Sys.time(), tutorial_id, \" (\", tutorial_version, \"): \", user_id , \"\\n\", sep = \"\")", "  cat(\"event: \", event, \"\\n\", sep = \"\")", "}", "options(tutorial.event_recorder = tutorial_event_recorder)", "", "options(tutorial.external.host = \"http://localhost:8080\")"), overwrite = FALSE)
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::store_exercise_setup_chunk("__setup__", c("# testing!", "x <- rnorm(1)"), overwrite = TRUE)
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::store_exercise_setup_chunk("__setup__", c("# testing!", "x <- rnorm(1)"), overwrite = TRUE)
</script>
```

If you delete the HTML file and run it again, you now get the wrong ordering, or `store` followed by `clear`.

```
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::store_exercise_setup_chunk("__setup__", c("# testing!", "x <- rnorm(1)"), overwrite = TRUE)
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::store_exercise_setup_chunk("__setup__", c("# testing!", "x <- rnorm(1)"), overwrite = TRUE)
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::register_http_handlers(session, metadata = NULL)
</script>
 
<script type="application/shiny-prerendered" data-context="server">
learnr:::clear_exercise_setup_chunks()
</script>
 ```

It looks like there's a difference in the order in which the initialization code runs the second time around that causes these problems. Thankfully, clicking "Run" in the IDE runs in a new process, so it wouldn't be vulnerable to this bug.

title: Include optional subsections (or dynamically skip subsections)
description:
Can we arrange for a set of sub-sections to be skipped or included based on whether or not the student answers an exercise (or exercises) correctly?

This may be a difficult ask because learnr documents are prerendered before a student submits exercise code. However, implementing the feature will allow us to: 

1. Create tutorials that dynamically adapt to a student's needs by digging deeper into areas where the student is having trouble and skimming over areas that the student has already mastered. In short, the feature will make learnr a more effective learning tool.

2. Create quizzes that quickly zero in on the student's skill level. The learnr document itself could be used as a quiz that uses an algorithm similar to binary search to quickly assess the student's skill level. This practice is common and is implemented, for example, in the GRE.

Both cases would likely require #358 to automate inclusion/exclusion based on student performance.

2. **Provide customized feedback in its response** (e.g. The last three exercises dealt with the dplyr mutate function. Since the student got them all wrong, I will suggest that the student take the remedial mutate() tutorial in my reply, and I will provide a link to that tutorial.)

title: Trigger actions when student advances between sections
description:
I'm settling more and more on tutorials that use progressive reveal (`progressive: true` in the YAML) displayed within or alongside the IDE. When combined with functionality with the `rstudioapi` package, this provides a convenient way to teach students not just how to write code, but also how to interact with the IDE.

**For these tutorials, it would be incredibly useful to trigger code whenever a student advances from one subsection to the next.** i.e. it would be incredibly useful to provide code that is run when a subsection begins (`pre`) and/or to provide code that is run when a section ends (`post`).

Here is an example use case:

1. The student clicks the "Continue" button to move to the next subsection, which will introduce the `mpg` dataset. The subsections that follow will also discuss the `mpg` dataset. I would like to display the dataset in a way that persists as the student moves from subsection to subsection. I would also like to familiarize the student with the RStudio IDE data viewer.

2. I have provided the following code for learnr to run when the tutorial advances to the new subsection, `rstudioapi::sendToConsole("View(ggplot2::mpg)", echo = FALSE, focus = FALSE)`.  I've provided it as an R code chunk with a special label, or a special option, or I've provided it in `{` after the subsection title, or by some other documented method

3. learnr runs the code as it advances to the new subsection, which opens `mpg` in the data viewer.

title: Enable tutorial.error.checker to provide checks on error
description: If a student submits code that throws an error, learnr exits the checking routine and displays the error message. This short circuit prevents the checking code from telling the student anything useful about what might have gone wrong. In short, the student is left to decipher the error message on his or her own. This is necessary when the checking code relies on the result of the student code (if it throws an error, there is no result). But it is a missed opportunity when the checking code parses the unevaluated student code, as `gradethis::grade_code()` does. Here is an example, `grade_code()` would return `"I expected mtcars where you wrote mt"` but learnr displays the error message. (code appended at bottom) To fix this, I suggest that we: 1. Add a `tutorials.error.checker` option that can be set to a grading function to run in the event that the student code throws an error. This option can be set in the same manner as the `tutorials.exercise.checker` option. It should be set to a function that can grade the student code without evaluating it, similar to `gradethis::grade_code()`. 2. Display the result of the error checking function beneath the error message. Here is a mock up. Code to recreate existing example above **** ```` --- title: "Example" output: learnr::tutorial runtime: shiny_prerendered --- ```{r setup, include=FALSE} library(learnr) library(gradethis) tutorial_options(exercise.checker = gradethis::grade_learnr) knitr::opts_chunk$set(out.width = "100%") ``` ## Welcome ### `mtcars` To see the `mtcars` data frame, type `mtcars` in the code block below and click "Submit Answer". ```{r ex, exercise = TRUE} ``` ```{r ex-solution} mtcars ``` ```{r ex-check} grade_code("Good job!") ``` ````

title: -code-check chunk does not trigger inclusion of a Submit Answer button
description: If I want to run a single check function that is run before the code is evaluated, I place it in a code chunk whose label is suffixed with `-code-check` per #2. title: All exercises resolve to complete when one is completed
description:
If you create two exercises and put `Sys.sleep(10); print("DONE!")` inside of each, then click "Run Code" on one, wait a few seconds, and then click "Run Code" on the other, you'll see that as soon as the first one resolves, both of them appear to be done (no more spinner on "Run Code", the button and results aren't grayed out, etc.) Then the second one eventually resolves and its output will appear too.

So the behavior is correct except that the "loading" status resolves prematurely for the exercise that's the last to finish.

title: Documentation - Tell users to not include .html tutorial files
description:
So, I'm primarily an educator, but I've been inspired by rstudio::conf to try turning my learnr tutorials into packages so I can more easily pass them out to students and include their assets (e.g. images, data) and dependencies.

I'm getting a bit hung up on whether I need to be including or ignoring .Rmd and .html files...

- learnr documentation indicates "Render your tutorial .Rmd to .html and include the rendered HTML in your R package"  (and `learner::run_tutorial()` says something similar)
- Looking at how `usethis::tutorial()` works, it adds the .Rmd for the tutorial to `.Rbuildignore`

These seem to suggest that I should be putting the rendered .html in my package.

However,
- `usethis::tutorial()` adds the .html files to `.gitignore`, so, at least for people installing my package off of GitHub, the .html files won't be available
- the `learnr` `.Rbuildignore` file has the .html files, not .Rmd (`^inst/tutorials/.*\.html$`)
- when I install `learnr`, the .Rmd files (from the example tutorials) are what end up on my computer (and if the .html files get installed, I haven't found them)
- After some (non-exaustive) tests, including the .Rmd files and excluding the .html files seems to work just fine

Given all of this, I would conclude that I should just include the .Rmd files rather than the .html files, except the `learnr` documentation makes it sound like the wrong thing to do, and I'm inclined to listen since I'm new to this.

It sounds like there was some discussion of this in conjunction with `usethis` (https://github.com/r-lib/usethis/issues/782), so it may just be that `learnr` documentation needs updating?  At any rate, I'd appreciate some clarity on what should be included in my package and what exactly I should add to my `.gitignore` and `.Rbuildignore` files.

If this is a `learnr` documentation issue, perhaps merge with https://github.com/rstudio/learnr/issues/254?

title: Embed a mechanism to enable iframe resizing to host page
description:
The [iframeResizer](https://github.com/davidjbradshaw/iframe-resizer) JS library contains a two-part solution that posts messages between the host page and the iframe contents.

If `learnr` embeds the [iframeResizer.contentWindow.min.js](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidjbradshaw/iframe-resizer/master/js/iframeResizer.contentWindow.min.js) then the hosting page can embed the [iframeResizer.min.js](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidjbradshaw/iframe-resizer/master/js/iframeResizer.min.js).

If we also get `pkgdown` to embed the `iframeResizer.min.js` component, then the resizing will happen out of the box for all `pkgdown` sites that embed tutorials.

I have a working prototype of this for the exercises at https://sys-admin-training.netlify.com/

title: Quiz questions are not loading when using multiple tabs
description:
reprex:
* Open many tutorials on shinyapps.io on different tabs.
* The first tutorial will work fine. Other tutorials will have problems advancing or saving progress (or any tutorial state) to the browser.

The tutorial tabs are all using `localforage` to access the `indexeddb` in the web browser.  This DB only allows for a single connection per browser.  Once the tab closes, that connection is released and the remaining tabs attempt to connect.

There is no warning or error.  

This problem exists in v0.9.2, but the quiz questions would display before any answers were being restored.  We could do this, but opted not to, as changing the UI after some non trivial time has passed is confusing.  (The downside is that some tabs can not display their quiz questions.)

Original note: https://github.com/rstudio/learnr/blob/fe4fe442850324dc17ef8aa9d645396ad8a2fbea/inst/lib/tutorial/tutorial.js#L1454-L1457

With `indexeddb` being [widely supported](https://caniuse.com/#search=indexeddb) (95%+), it could be used natively and `localforage` could be dropped as our requirements are slim (essentially key/value lookup).  `localstorage` could also be used instead, but there is a limitation of 5mb per domain.  `indexeddb` would be best going forward.

Known issues:
* https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51615658/using-indexeddb-operation-in-multiple-tabs
* https://github.com/localForage/localForage/issues/912
* https://github.com/localForage/localForage/issues/179
  * using `this.localforage._dbInfo.db.close()` does close the connection. However, the connection was not allowed to reconnect. 😞

title: Correct message displays for incorrect answers when type = "multiple"
description:
If you add `type = "multiple"` to a `question()` than any message attached to the correct answer will display for every answer. It should only display if the correct answer is one of the answers selected. This affects the Welcome > Is this tutorial for you? Quiz in the `ex-setup-r` tutorial, and probably others. The document below reproduces.

````
---
title: "Tutorial"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
```

## Topic 1

### Exercise 

Here everything works fine. The message "You chose C!" only appears if you choose C.

```{r question}
question("Choose C",
    answer("A"),
    answer("B"),
    answer("C", correct = TRUE, message = "You chose C!"),
    answer("D")
)
```

Here things break because we added `type = "multiple"`. Now the message "You chose C!" appears no matter what you choose.

```{r question-2}
question("Choose C",
    answer("A"),
    answer("B"),
    answer("C", correct = TRUE, message = "You chose C!"),
    answer("D"),
    type = "multiple"
)
```
````

title: Feature Request: serverless questions?
description:
Hi there! 

Thanks for making `learnr`, such a neat package with a great interface!

I'd like to be able to include simple multi-choice, true false, or even string match questions in various html places - such as bookdown/presentations/html.

At the moment this becomes challenging with `learnr` as you need to have a server to serve up the questions.

What I want is a way to ask people an MCQ question, and then for a radio button interface to be presented, which knows if it is right or wrong - I'm not interested in storing this information anywhere, just present the question - basically I want to use the same interface that `learnr` provides: https://community.rstudio.com/t/create-questions-and-quiz-in-learnr-rmarkdown-document/17951

```{r quiz1, echo=FALSE}
quiz(caption = "Quiz 1",
  question("What number is the letter A in the *English* alphabet?",
    answer("8"),
    answer("14"),
    answer("1", correct = TRUE),
    answer("23")
  ),
  question("Where are you right now? (select ALL that apply)",
    answer("Planet Earth", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Pluto"),
    answer("At a computing device", correct = TRUE),
    answer("In the Milky Way", correct = TRUE),
    incorrect = "Incorrect. You're on Earth, in the Milky Way, at a computer."
  )
)
```

I understand that this might be out of scope for `learnr`, so I am very happy to spin this out into it's own light-weight package, but I thought that I should check here before I do that, in case it is something you have thought about or feel is in scope?

title: Documentation: reframe "Publishing" section in terms of use cases
description:
The "Publishing" section of the pkgdown website would be more useful to users if it was framed in terms of the needs of the users of learnr tutorials. We (@mine-cetinkaya-rundel @jules32 @isteves and I) thought of three users:

1. Instructor who sends students to a Shiny web link to run the tutorial through their browser (perhaps, using the free academic version of Shiny Server)
2. Instructor who wants students to install a tutorials package, and do `run_tutorial()` locally
3. Package developer who wants to include a learnr tutorial in their package to demonstrate how to use it

The recommended publishing route in each of these cases would then be:

1. Deploy on shinyapps.io / Shiny Server 
2. / 3. Include one or multiple learnr tutorials in an R package

We are thus proposing replacing in the [Publishing section](https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/index.html#publishing):

> The most straightforward way to deploy a tutorial is to include it within an R package and have users run it directly via the  learnr::run_tutorial function.

With something like:

> "If you would like to provide a browser link for students to use your learnr tutorial without further configuration on their end, do X. If you would like students to download a package so that they can run tutorials locally, do Y. If you want to include a learnr tutorial in your existing package to teach users how to use it, do Z."

title: Feature request: ask to install tutorial dependencies
description:
Hi! @jules32, @angela-li, and I are working on improving the `use_tutorial()` function for `usethis`, which sets up the `learnr` tutorial package format . Our two main use cases are (1) package developers that want to include tutorials as documentation and (2) course instructors that want to distribute a bundle of tutorials to students.

For course instructors, it's especially important to minimize friction related to package installs. Thus, it would be great if `run_tutorial()` would prompt the user to install packages that the tutorial depends on.  

@cderv recommended 3 options to find the dependencies in the tutorial:

- [`renv::dependencies()`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/reference/dependencies.html) - returns a list of dependencies contained in a file/folder
- [`attachment::att_from_rmds()`](https://thinkr-open.github.io/attachment/) - returns a list of dependencies contained in a file/folder
- [`rsconnect::appDependencies()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/rsconnect/man/appDependencies.html) - returns a *full tree* of dependencies contained in a file/folder

`utils::menu()` could then be used to ask users if it's okay to install all the dependencies.

title: Support test-driven development style of questions and solutions
description:
(following discussion with @schloerke - please correct if I've misunderstood)

I want to be able to ask a learner to write some code and provide them with a set of assertions that the finished code has to pass that they can see, and another set that it also has to pass that they can't see. The first set helps clarify the exercise goals, and shows them what test-driven development looks like. The second set of checks (hidden from them) is necessary so that they don't just write "if inputs 1 then print solution 1, if inputs 2 then print solution 2".

My suggestion was to allow multiple `-check` blocks for each exercise and use `include=TRUE` and `include=FALSE` to control which the learner could see. @schloerke believes we can get the same effect with much less disruption by writing a slightly more sophisticated equivalent to `strict_check` and/or `grade_learnr`.

title: Setup chunks should be available to solutions
description:
We are writing a tutorial where the students are often, but not always using a data frame that should already be in the workspace.  To do this, for the students' code, we have an exercise `my-exercise` that has `exercise.setup="get-the-data"`, where `get-the-data` is a setup chunk that loads the data.

Of course the solution needs the same data, but it seems that adding `exercise.setup="get-the-data"` does not work as an option to `my-exercise-solution`.

I think the setup for the exercise should be available to the solution by default.   At least, it should be possible to pass the setup to the solution code. title: Feature request: Extend multiple choice question grading paradigm to code exercises
description:
After experimenting with writing a [code grading package](https://github.com/rstudio-education/grader), I think the most flexible way to provide easy-to-use grading tools is to recreate the multiple choice grading scheme for code exercises (and also for fill-in-the-blank exercises).

## Goal

The goal is to let tutorial authors list likely code results (including the correct result), and to assign a custom message to be displayed for each result. When a student clicks Submit Code, learnr will evaluate the code and match the student result against the enumerated results. 

* If a match is found, learnr will display the message associated with the match. 
* If a match is not found, learnr will display a default message. 
* If the student code returns an error, the error is displayed in the learnr tutorial (alternatively/eventually authors will be able to match errors with custom messages to display).

## Requirements (suggested)

1. A function that authors can call in the `-check` chunk that accompanies an exercise. This function is an analogue to the `question()` function for multiple choice questions. I'll call it `match_result()` below, but we can choose a better name. 

    Where sensible, `match_result()` should repeat the arguments of `question()` (e.g. `allow_retry` and `incorrect` (which provides the default message to display if none of the enumerated results are matched)).

2. A function that can be passed to `match_result()`. This function is an analogue to `answer()` Authors can use it to list possible results for a code exercise. I'll call this function `result()`. 

    `result()` should differ from `answer()` in that the author can pass an R object, instead of a character string, to the first argument of `result()` (we should check for NSE issues here). 

    `result()` should resemble `answer()` in that the author can use the arguments of `result()` to identify the correct result and to provide a message to display if the student result matches the result. 

    Preferably, `answer()` and `result()` can be combined into the same function, but I do not know if that is possible.

3. A "`collect`" argument for `match_result()`. This argument should default to `NULL`, but should accept an R expression (as a character string?) to be provided by the tutorial author. When `collect` does not equal `NULL`, learnr should run the provided code on the exercise environment as it is after the student code has been evaluated. `match_result()` will then match the result of the `collect` expression against the enumerated results. This argument is designed to help authors fetch the results of exercises that involve creating objects, defining functions, etc. 

    When `collect = NULL`, `match_result()` will match the result returned by the student code against the enumerated results.

    If `collect = NULL` and the student code does not return a result, `match_result()` should display a message like "I did not notice a result. Does your code return one?"

4. If the student response is empty, `match_result()` should return a message like "I did not see your code. Did you write any?"

5. When run, `match_result()` should enter an event with the learnr event recorder. The event should capture the student ID, the exercise label, possibly the student code, and definitely the outcome: correct or incorrect.

## Example UI

Here's an example of how this would look in tutorial .Rmd

### Exercise 1

* Create an object named `x`. Assign into it the result of `1 + 1`. Then click Submit Answer

````
```{r ex1, exercise = TRUE}

```
````

````
```{r ex1-solution}
x <- 1 + 1
```
````

````
```{r ex1-check}
y <- list(a = list(1, 2), b = TRUE)

match_result(collect = "x",
             result(2, correct = TRUE, "Good Job! 1 + 1 = 2."),
             result(3, "1 + 1 does not equal three. Check your work. I think you made a typo."),
             result(0, "Did you write one _minus_ one?"),
             result(y, "Wow. If you can create hierarchical lists, you should probably skip to the next tutorial."),
             incorrect = "That is not the correct answer.",
             allow_retry = TRUE)
```
````
## Commentary

The advantage of this approach is that the tools will be simple to use and robust. Authors can re-apply their knowledge of multiple choice questions to grading code exercises.

The disadvantage is that the tools cannot tell the student _why_ they got a wrong answer unless the author identifies the student's failure mode (and the associated result) ahead of time. However, authors should be able to spot and check for common mistakes (especially after they review the initial round of tutorial logs).

I've made good progress writing a [code checker](https://github.com/rstudio-education/grader) that can analyze user code itself and return a sensible message in most cases. However, I believe it will take an order of magnitude more development time to make checking code (instead of results) robust. If we leave in the checking hooks, users can choose to develop and use such a checker at their discretion.

title: Incorrect initialization of tutorial yaml metadata
description:
The [tutorial identifiers](https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/publishing.html#tutorial_identifiers) documentation states that it's possible to modify the `id` and `version` of a tutorial: ```yaml --- title: "Hello, Tutorial!" tutorial: id: "com.example.tutorials.my-first-tutorial" version: 2.1 --- ``` Furthermore, you can access these values by [Recording events](https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/publishing.html#recording_events). However, when trying this, it doesn't work, and the yaml header is ignored. Here is a reprex. When running this tutorial, it prints the id, version and user to stdout: 
---
title: "learnr test"
output: learnr::tutorial
runtime: shiny_prerendered
tutorial:
  id: "toytorial"
  version: "0.1"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
tutorial_options(exercise.eval = FALSE)

new_recorder <- function(tutorial_id, tutorial_version, user_id, event, data) {
    cat(tutorial_id, " (", tutorial_version, "): ", user_id, "\n", sep = "")
}

options(tutorial.event_recorder = new_recorder)
```

### Test yourself

Use `dim()` command to get the dimensions of 'iris'.

```{r, ex1, exercise=TRUE, echo = FALSE}
```
However, I get these results: ``` Listening on http://127.0.0.1:3492 C:/Users/apdev/Documents/temp (1.0): apdev ``` Clearly the version and id are not honoured. Pull request following.

description:
I've noticed that the code run in learnr exercise chunks has access to different environments depending on how the tutorial is launched. I expected the code in the exercise chunks to only have access to objects that are created in the setup chunks that are associated with the exercises (as well as the global setup chunk). I see different behavior in two cases:

1. Exercise chunks inherit the global environment of the local R session from which the tutorial is launched when the tutorial is launched from the command line with `learnr::run_tutorial()`. By this I mean that code run in the exercise chunks can use objects stored in the local global environment.

2. Exercise chunks inherit the knit environment of the document that they appear in when tutorial is launched with the GUI Run Document button. By this I mean that code run in an exercise chunk can use objects created in any of the document's normal knitr chunks. This may have something to do with pre-rendering because I do not notice the behavior the first time that I run the document, but on every subsequent run. So far, I've only seen this in local mode (launched from GUI), not on tutorials published on shinyapps.io.

I've hosted a learnr tutorial that describes and demo's these bugs in an attempt to provide a reproducible example: https://tutorials.shinyapps.io/scoping-rules/

title: Feature request: text input fields for student answers
description:
I would like to build exercises that use the equivalent of Shiny's numeric input and text input widgets to collect student responses. For example, I would like to write a prompt and then insert a text field for the student to write in, e.g.

> Which species of iris has the largest average petal length?
> TEXT FIELD

Ideally, I could supply answer() options as with question(). The text box would match student submissions to answers, ignoring case, whitespace, and misspellings(?). learnr would return the message associated with the matched answer (as well as the correct = ? status). If the submission is not matched to an answer(), learnr would return the general message provided to the text box.

One immediate application for this would be to transition students from the learnr tutorial environment to the full-blown IDE. Students could do their work in the IDE and then submit their "answer" in the text box for grading. A second application would be case studies (which would also require work in the IDE).

It is possible to tell the student to write text in the existing exercise box, but explaining this would be a distraction to the lesson (and may break the checker function).
